$comment: Frozen, synthetic Horizon fixtures for the fault and pagination suite. No production wallet, transaction, or payment data appears here: every address, hash, and amount is generated from a fixed seed and is recognisably synthetic. See docs/testing-horizon.md before changing anything in this file.
generatedFrom: deterministic seed; contains no recorded production traffic

empty-page.description: An account with no payment history. One empty page, no next link.

empty-embedded-absent.description: A 200 whose body omits _embedded entirely. Treated as an empty feed, not as corruption — Horizon answers this way for an unused account.

single-page.description: Three records, no next link. The feed ends on the first page.

multi-page.description: Three full pages walked by cursor, then a terminal page with no next link. Each step asserts the cursor the client sent.

repeated-cursor.description: Horizon hands back a next cursor it has already issued. Following it would loop forever, so the walk stops and reports repeated_cursor.

self-referential-cursor.description: The next cursor equals the cursor just used. The degenerate form of a loop.

overlapping-pages.description: Page two repeats two records from page one, as a ledger reorganisation or a lagging read replica would. The overlap must be deduplicated by operation id, not counted twice.

fully-replayed-page.description: Page two is byte-identical to page one but advances the cursor. Every record is a duplicate and nothing new is accumulated.

rate-limited-then-ok.description: 429 with Retry-After, then success. Transient: the retry must honour the header rather than the client's own backoff.

rate-limited-exhausted.description: 429 on every attempt. The retry budget runs out and the fault surfaces.

rate-limited-absurd-retry-after.description: 429 asking for a 3600-second wait. Honouring it verbatim would hang the caller far past any request deadline, so the delay is capped.

timeout-then-ok.description: The first attempt times out; the retry succeeds.

timeout-exhausted.description: Every attempt times out. Transient, but the budget is finite.

server-error-then-ok.description: 503 then success — the ordinary Horizon blip.

server-error-mid-walk.description: Page one succeeds, page two fails twice then succeeds. The retry budget is per page, so page two still gets its full allowance.

network-error-then-ok.description: The connection fails outright, then recovers.

fails-on-second-page.description: Page one succeeds, page two exhausts its retries. Used to prove the first page's cursor is still usable to resume from.

resume-from-cursor.description: A read that starts from a supplied cursor. The first request must already carry it.

expired-cursor.description: Horizon rejects the cursor with 400. Permanent for that cursor: retrying it cannot work, so it must not consume the retry budget.

gone-cursor.description: 410 for a cursor aged out of Horizon's retention. Also permanent.

account-not-found.description: 404 for an unknown account. Permanent; never retried.

malformed-page-body.description: A 200 whose body is a JSON array rather than a Horizon collection. Permanent for the page — a retry returns the same nonsense.

unparseable-body.description: A 200 with a body that is not JSON at all.

malformed-records.description: One page mixing valid records with permanently invalid ones: a missing id, a missing amount, a non-numeric amount, an unparseable date, a null entry, and a non-native asset with no code. Each is skipped and counted; none aborts the page and none is retried.

non-payment-records.description: Well-formed records that are not incoming payments: an outgoing payment, a create_account operation, and a payment addressed to a different account. Ordinary, not faults — they are filtered without being counted as malformed.

endless-pages.description: Horizon never stops offering a next cursor. Only the page bound ends the walk. Twelve pages are scripted so a ten-page bound is reached with room to spare.

time-bounded.description: Records straddle a time boundary. Pages are newest-first, so once a record precedes the boundary nothing later can be in range and the walk stops.
